    ..row([TCB #h(4pt) #text(size: 8pt)[(per thread)]], [register context, priority, quantum]),
    ..row([Kernel Stack #h(4pt) #text(size: 8pt)[(per thread)]], [separate; needed for kernel re-entry]),
    ..row([PCB #h(4pt) #text(size: 8pt)[(per process)]], [address-space map, handles]),
  )),
)

Every thread also has a dedicated kernel stack (typically 4–12 KB). Because a context switch can occur even while the thread is executing kernel-mode code, the kernel cannot use a shared stack; each thread must have its own place to save its kernel-mode state.

docs.title: Thread Local Storage (TLS)
docs.text:
Global variables are shared across all threads in a process. TLS provides the escape hatch: a variable declared in TLS has one independent copy per thread, invisible to all other threads.

The TEB's TLS pointer is the fast path to that per-thread storage. The C runtime (_beginthreadex / the CRT startup) initializes TLS slots before the thread's entry function runs, which is one reason to prefer CRT thread creation functions over raw OS calls when using the standard library.

A typical use case is a per-thread error code (errno in the CRT, for example) — each thread reads and writes its own copy without locks.

docs.title: Fibers: User-Mode Threads
docs.text:
Windows also exposes Fibers — execution contexts that look like threads to the code running in them, but are scheduled entirely by the application, not the OS.

Key properties:

  • The OS knows nothing about fibers; the scheduler sees only the kernel thread that hosts them.
  • Switching between fibers is cooperative (the running fiber must explicitly yield).
  • A context switch between fibers is cheap: it is a pure user-mode register save/restore, with no kernel transition.
  • Fibers are vulnerable to the same blocking problem as user-level threads generally: if the host thread blocks on a kernel wait (I/O, mutex), all fibers on that thread block with it.

Fibers predate modern async/await patterns and are rarely the right tool today, but they illustrate the broader principle of user-mode scheduling.

docs.title: Kernel-Level vs. User-Level Threads
docs.text:
The distinction between kernel-level and user-level threads is architectural, not Windows-specific.

Property Kernel-Level Thread User-Level Thread Scheduler visibility Kernel sees each thread individually Kernel sees only the process I/O block behavior Only the blocked thread stops; others run Entire process blocks if any thread blocks Context switch cost Higher — requires user↔kernel mode transition Lower — no mode switch within the process Parallelism on multi-core True parallel execution across cores Limited to one core per process (without hybrid mapping)

Kernel-level threads are what Windows and Linux implement natively. The kernel's scheduler distributes CPU time directly to threads; if thread A blocks on I/O, thread B in the same process can immediately receive the CPU.

User-level threads (green threads, fibers, coroutines) live entirely in user space. The process manages its own internal schedule. The advantage is cheaper switching; the cost is that a single blocking syscall stalls all user-level threads in that process because the kernel only sees one schedulable entity.

docs.title: Process vs. Thread: The Cost Dimension
docs.text:
The performance difference between process-level and thread-level context switching follows directly from address-space ownership.

Switching between two threads in the same process:

  • Save/restore register set (TCB swap).
  • No address-space change — page tables stay the same.
  • TLB and CPU cache remain warm.
  • Relatively cheap.

Switching between threads in different processes:

  • Save/restore register set.
  • Load new CR3 (page-table base) — the entire virtual address mapping changes.
  • TLB flush: cached virtual→physical translations are now invalid.
  • Cache pressure: the new process's working set is cold; L1/L2 misses spike.
  • Significantly more expensive.

This cost asymmetry is the primary reason multi-threaded designs are preferred over multi-process designs for tightly coupled work: threads amortize the address-space overhead across all their parallelism.

The flip side is isolation: a buggy thread can corrupt the entire process heap; a buggy child process cannot touch the parent. The choice between processes and threads is always a trade-off between isolation and performance.

docs.title: Kernel vs. User Mode: Why It Matters for Thread Switching
docs.text:
The CPU operates in (at least) two privilege rings:

  • User mode (Ring 3): restricted instructions; cannot access kernel memory.
  • Kernel mode (Ring 0): unrestricted; full access to hardware and kernel data.

A kernel mode switch (also called a mode transition) happens on every syscall or hardware interrupt. The thread does not change — it is still running — but its privilege level rises to Ring 0 so it can execute kernel code. The SYSCALL / INT 2E instruction triggers this transition.

A context switch is different: the executing thread changes. The Dispatcher (a software-interrupt routine in the Windows kernel) saves the current TCB and loads another. Context switches happen when a thread's quantum expires or when it voluntarily blocks.

Both cost something. A kernel mode switch costs a register save and a privilege-level change. A context switch costs that plus, potentially, the full address-space overhead described above.

docs.title: The GIL is a lock on bytecode execution, not a ban on threads
docs.text:
Python threads are real OS threads — the same kernel-scheduled entities std::thread wraps. The Global Interpreter Lock does not change that; it admits one thread executing Python bytecode at a time. It is a lock, not a core affinity: the holder runs on whatever core the scheduler picked, and threads migrate across cores over their lifetime. "Python runs on one core" is the observed effect, not the mechanism, and the difference matters because the lock is released around blocking I/O and inside C extensions. Threaded numpy work and threaded I/O really do use several cores from one process. The constraint is narrower than it sounds: pure-Python compute cannot run in parallel within a process.

It is tempting to group GIL-limited threading with coroutines, since both multiplex many logical tasks onto one core's worth of execution. That shared axis is real, but the mechanism separating them is the one that predicts the bugs:

who decides the switch parallelism OS threads under a GIL the OS preempts — timer expiry or on I/O I/O and native code only coroutines (asyncio, Unity IEnumerator) the code, at an explicit yield / await never separate processes the OS, with independent interpreters real

Preemption can cut between any two bytecodes; a cooperative yield cannot. That single fact is why threaded code needs locks around shared mutable state and coroutine code mostly does not — the coroutine author knows every point at which control can leave.

The cross-language mapping is easy to get backwards. A Unity coroutine's counterpart is asyncio, not threading: IEnumerator/yield driven by the engine's update loop, no threads involved at any point. And Unity coroutines are the outlier within .NET itself — C#'s Task/async dispatches onto a real thread pool with genuine multicore parallelism, so async in C# and async in Python read alike and differ fundamentally underneath. Syntactic resemblance across languages says nothing about which of the three rows above you are in.

Open: CPU-bound loop across 1 vs 4 threads, default build vs free-threaded build, with multiprocessing as the control.

Study notes — Windows-specific material based on 윤성우, 《윈도우즈 시스템 프로그래밍》 (book + lectures).

docs.title: Synchronization and Deadlock
docs.text: Concurrent threads share memory and devices. That sharing is precisely what makes them useful — and precisely what makes them dangerous. This post covers the core problem (race conditions), the concept that solves it (critical sections and mutual exclusion), the three main primitives that enforce that concept, the deeper essence of what synchronization is trying to achieve, and finally deadlock: when the cure becomes the disease.

docs.title: Race Conditions
docs.text:
A race condition occurs when the correctness of a program depends on the relative timing of two or more threads, and that timing is not controlled.

The canonical example is a shared counter:

// Thread A and Thread B both execute this:
g_count++;

g_count++ looks like one operation, but it compiles to three:

// 1. Load g_count into a register
// 2. Increment the register
// 3. Store the register back to g_count

If Thread A reads g_count = 5, gets preempted after step 1, Thread B then reads 5, increments to 6, stores 6, and Thread A resumes and also stores 6 — the net result is 6 instead of 7. One increment was silently lost. This is a race condition: the outcome depends on who wins the CPU race.

The problem is not that threads run in parallel — it is that a logically atomic operation is not physically atomic. The scheduler can interrupt between any two machine instructions.

docs.title: Critical Sections and Mutual Exclusion
docs.text:
A critical section is any region of code that accesses a shared resource in a way that must not be interleaved with another thread doing the same. In the example above, the three-instruction sequence is the critical section.

Mutual exclusion (mutex) is the property that at most one thread executes a critical section at any given time. It is the minimal correctness requirement for shared-state concurrency.

Three classical requirements for a correct mutual exclusion solution:

  1. Mutual exclusion — at most one thread inside the critical section at a time.
  2. Progress — if no thread is in the critical section, a thread that wants to enter must eventually be allowed in (no indefinite blocking by outsiders).
  3. Bounded waiting — after a thread requests entry, there is a finite upper bound on how many times other threads may enter before it does (no starvation).

Software-only solutions (Peterson's algorithm, Dekker's algorithm) exist but are fragile on modern CPUs due to out-of-order execution and memory reordering. In practice, mutual exclusion is enforced with hardware-assisted primitives.

docs.title: Mutex (Mutual Exclusion Lock)
docs.text:
A mutex is the direct implementation of the critical section concept. It has two operations — lock (acquire) and unlock (release) — and one invariant: only the thread that locked it may unlock it.

mutex.lock();
// --- critical section ---
g_count++;
// --- end critical section ---
mutex.unlock();

When a thread calls lock() and the mutex is already held, the thread blocks: it is removed from the run queue and does not consume CPU until the mutex becomes available. This is what distinguishes a mutex from a spinlock (which busy-waits in a loop). Blocking gives up the CPU; spinning keeps it.

Ownership is the key property of a mutex: a mutex is held by exactly one thread, and that thread is responsible for releasing it.

docs.title: Semaphore
docs.text:
A semaphore generalizes the mutex. It holds an integer counter and exposes two operations:

  • wait (also called P, or acquire): decrement the counter; if the result is negative, block.
  • signal (also called V, or release): increment the counter; if any threads are waiting, wake one.

A binary semaphore (counter initialized to 1) behaves like a mutex. A counting semaphore (counter initialized to N) allows up to N threads to proceed concurrently — useful for resource pools (e.g., "at most 4 database connections at a time").

The critical difference from a mutex: a semaphore has no ownership. One thread can call wait, and a different thread can call signal. This makes semaphores useful for signaling (producer–consumer) rather than just mutual exclusion.

// Producer
produce_item();
sem.signal();    // announce that an item is ready

// Consumer
sem.wait();      // block until an item exists
consume_item();

docs.title: Condition Variable
docs.text:
A condition variable allows a thread to atomically release a mutex and block, waiting until another thread signals that a condition has changed. It is always used in conjunction with a mutex.

mutex.lock();
while (!condition_is_true()) {
    cond.wait(mutex);   // atomically releases mutex, blocks, re-acquires on wake
}
// proceed — condition is now true
mutex.unlock();

The while (not if) is essential: spurious wakeups are allowed by the specification, and between when a thread is woken and when it re-acquires the mutex, another thread may have consumed the resource. Always re-check the condition.

Condition variables are the standard building block for bounded buffers, thread pools, and any pattern where a thread must wait for a state change rather than just for exclusive access.

docs.title: The Essence of Synchronization
docs.text:
Synchronization is not primarily about locks. It is about two deeper guarantees:

  1. Atomicity — a sequence of operations that should appear indivisible does appear indivisible from all other threads.
  2. Visibility — when one thread writes a value, other threads that need to see it actually do, in the correct order.

Modern CPUs execute instructions out of order and cache writes locally. Without explicit synchronization primitives, there is no guarantee that a value written by Thread A is visible to Thread B at all, let alone in program order. Synchronization primitives act as memory barriers: they tell the CPU and the compiler that reorderings across this point are not permitted.

This is why even a simple flag like bool done = true is not safe without synchronization across threads: the store may be reordered, buffered in a store queue, or cached in a way that Thread B never sees. The primitive is not just about mutual exclusion — it is about making the memory model coherent.

docs.title: Deadlock
docs.text: Deadlock is what happens when synchronization is applied without discipline. Two or more threads each hold a resource and are each waiting for a resource held by the other. Neither can proceed. Neither will release. The system freezes.

docs.title: The Four Coffman Conditions
docs.text:
Deadlock can only occur if all four of the following conditions hold simultaneously:

  1. Mutual exclusion — resources cannot be shared; only one thread at a time.
  2. Hold and wait — a thread holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire others.
  3. No preemption — resources cannot be forcibly taken; a thread must release them voluntarily.
  4. Circular wait — there exists a cycle: Thread A waits for Thread B's resource, Thread B waits for Thread C's, ..., Thread N waits for Thread A's.

All four must hold. Breaking any one of them prevents deadlock.

docs.title: Breaking the Conditions
docs.text:
Break mutual exclusion: Make resources shareable. Only applicable to read-only resources (multiple threads can hold a read lock simultaneously). Not applicable to writable state.

Break hold and wait: Require threads to request all resources at once, before starting. If any resource is unavailable, the thread requests nothing and waits. This is conservative but safe. Alternatively, a thread that cannot acquire all resources releases the ones it already holds and retries.

Break no preemption: Allow the OS or runtime to forcibly revoke a resource from a thread. Practical for some resources (CPU time, locks with timeout), impractical for others (a half-written file).

Break circular wait: Impose a global ordering on all resources. Require every thread to acquire resources in that order. If Lock A always comes before Lock B in the ordering, no thread can hold B while waiting for A — the cycle is impossible by construction.

// All threads must acquire locks in order: mutex_A before mutex_B.
// This makes circular wait structurally impossible.
mutex_A.lock();
mutex_B.lock();
// ... work ...
mutex_B.unlock();
mutex_A.unlock();

The global ordering approach is the most commonly used technique in practice: define a lock hierarchy, enforce it in code review, document it as a constraint.

docs.title: Deadlock Avoidance vs. Prevention
docs.text:
• Prevention: structurally rule out one of the four conditions (as above). Static, conservative, always safe.
  • Avoidance: dynamically decide whether granting a request would lead to an unsafe state (e.g., Banker's Algorithm). Requires knowing maximum resource needs in advance — rarely practical in general-purpose software.
  • Detection and recovery: allow deadlock to occur, detect it (cycle detection in the resource-allocation graph), then recover by aborting or rolling back one thread. Used in databases (deadlock victim selection), not typical in systems programming.

In most application code, prevention via lock ordering is the right tool: cheap, static, and eliminates the problem entirely.

Study notes — Windows-specific material based on 윤성우, 《윈도우즈 시스템 프로그래밍》 (book + lectures).

docs.title: TLB, Page Faults, and Copy-on-Write
docs.text: Two corrections from a self-test on virtual memory. Both are places where a plausible mental model is wrong in a way that matters for performance work.

docs.title: A TLB miss is not a page fault
docs.text:
Three separate structures nest, and each has its own kind of miss.

  • Page table in RAM: the full virtual-to-physical map, one entry per 4 KB page, built by the OS.
  • TLB: a cache of a few hundred to ~1,500 recent page table entries inside the MMU. A subset, not "the process's page tables".
  • Data cache (L1/L2/L3): the bytes themselves. Unrelated to translation.

A load of virtual address X:

  1. Check the TLB. Hit: physical address known. Miss: on x86 a hardware page walker reads the page table from RAM, fills the TLB, continues. No trap, no OS involvement, a few memory accesses.
  2. Entry says present: fetch the data, which can itself hit or miss L1/L2/L3.
  3. Entry says not present: page fault. CPU raises exception 14 (#PF), the OS loads from disk, allocates a zero page, or kills the process with a segfault.
Miss Fixed by Cost TLB miss Hardware page walk nanoseconds Data cache miss Hardware fetch from RAM tens of ns Page fault OS handler µs to ms

"Miss" sounds like failure. It means "not cached". The TLB never decides validity; the page table entry does. The wrong model, where a TLB miss traps to the OS, describes software-managed TLBs (MIPS, older SPARC), not x86 or ARM.

Open: how much do 2 MB huge pages cut dTLB-load-misses for a process with tens of GB of resident weights?

docs.title: fork copies nothing, but in CPython reading is writing
docs.text:
After fork, the child does not share memory logically. It has its own address space. The OS points both page tables at the same physical frames and marks every page read-only. Extra RAM right after fork is the new page tables, a few MB for an 8 GB parent.

The first write to a page from either side faults on the read-only bit. The OS copies that one 4 KB page and gives the writer its own. This is copy-on-write.

The Python-specific trap: a worker that only reads still increments a refcount in every object header it touches. That is a write. A read-only worker therefore copies every page holding an object it looks at, and slowly duplicates most of the parent. This is why multiprocessing with a large loaded model bloats, and why the fixes are fork before loading, shared memory, or gc.freeze().

Open: measure it. Fork an 8 GB Python process, walk a list in the child, watch RSS.

docs.title: Two answers that were right, with one refinement each
docs.text:
mmap of a 10 GB file barely moves RSS. Demand paging: the mapping creates page table entries marked not present. First touch of each page faults, the OS reads that 4 KB, RSS grows one page.

write() returns, power dies one second later. Data is in the page cache, not on disk, unless fsync (FlushFileBuffers on Windows) was called. Refinement: the kernel flushes dirty pages on a timer, roughly every 30 s by default, not only on eviction. The window is seconds, not indefinite. Databases fsync on every commit for exactly this reason.

docs.title: Claude Code + AI Harness Setup (macOS)
docs.text:
This guide rebuilds my full AI coding environment on macOS as of August 2026. It goes well beyond a bare Claude Code install: the working setup is a harness — Claude Code at the center, extended by the oh-my-claudecode plugin (multi-agent orchestration), the Codex CLI as a token-offload second engine, the rtk proxy for token-efficient shell output, Serena for semantic code navigation, and skills for repeatable workflows.

The February 2026 version of this guide described four MCP servers (Sequential Thinking, GitHub, Sentry, Serena) on a stock install. Sequential Thinking is superseded by built-in extended thinking, and hosted connectors (GitHub, Slack, Notion, Google Drive…) are now managed from the Claude app side rather than hand-added MCP endpoints. This rewrite documents what I actually run.

docs.title: 1. Claude Code CLI
docs.text:
# Prerequisites (see Mac_dev_setup.md): brew, uv, node

# Claude desktop app (GUI) — optional but useful
brew install --cask claude

# Claude Code CLI — native binary, self-updating
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

# Verify — installs to ~/.local/bin/claude
claude --version

Desktop app vs CLI: brew install --cask claude installs Claude.app (GUI). The Claude Code CLI (claude in the terminal) is a separate native binary from the curl script. They share your Claude account but update independently.

# First run — follow the login prompts
claude

Log in with a Claude account (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise) unless you specifically want API-metered billing via Anthropic Console.

docs.title: 2. Plugins
docs.text:
Plugins are the biggest change since early 2026 — they bundle agents, skills, hooks, and MCP servers into installable units. Manage them with /plugin inside Claude Code.

My enabled set:

Plugin Marketplace What it adds oh-my-claudecode omc Multi-agent orchestration: specialized agents (executor, architect, verifier…), execution modes (autopilot, ralph, ultrawork), team pipelines, HUD statusline codex openai-codex Bridges the Codex CLI as a rescue/second-opinion subagent warp claude-code-warp Warp terminal integration

Inside Claude Code:

/plugin
# → Browse marketplaces → add the marketplace → install → enable

oh-my-claudecode also has a guided setup — after installing, just say "setup omc" in a session and it configures its hooks, HUD, and state directories itself.

docs.title: 3. Codex CLI (Second Engine)
docs.text:
The Codex CLI runs OpenAI models with its own context window. I use it as a token offload: bulk file reading, self-contained lookups, and second opinions run in Codex so the file contents never enter Claude's context — only the conclusion comes back.

# The codex cask bundles the CLI
brew install --cask codex

# Log in (ChatGPT account — no API key needed)
codex login

# Verify
codex --version

The core pattern — read-only, self-contained prompts whose return value is the answer:

codex exec --sandbox read-only "Summarize what this repo's scripts/ directory does. Reply with one line per script."

Mark trusted repos in ~/.codex/config.toml so codex exec runs there without prompts. Rules I follow: Codex never touches secrets, and anything needing conversation context gets that context paraphrased into the prompt (Codex starts blank every call).

docs.title: 4. rtk (Token Proxy)
docs.text:
rtk ("Rust Token Killer") wraps common CLI commands (git status, ls, test runners…) and returns compressed, token-efficient output — 60–90% savings on routine dev operations. A Claude Code PreToolUse hook rewrites commands to pass through rtk transparently.

brew install rtk

# Verify — should print savings analytics, not "command not found"
rtk gain

Name collision: if rtk gain fails, you may have installed a different rtk (Rust Type Kit). Check which rtk and the formula source.

The hook lives in ~/.claude/settings.json under hooks.PreToolUse; oh-my-claudecode's setup wires it. Useful meta-commands: rtk gain --history (per-command savings), rtk discover (finds missed opportunities in your Claude Code history).

docs.title: 5. MCP Servers
docs.text: My current MCP philosophy: fewer, scoped, project-level where possible. Hosted integrations (Slack, Notion, Google Drive, Gmail…) come through Claude-app connectors automatically; hand-configured MCP servers are only for things connectors don't cover.

docs.title: Serena (semantic code navigation) — per-project
docs.text:
Serena provides LSP-backed symbol search, references, and precise edits. I register it per project in a committed .mcp.json rather than globally — projects that don't need it don't pay its startup cost:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "serena": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": [
        "--from", "git+https://github.com/oraios/serena",
        "serena", "start-mcp-server", "--context", "ide-assistant"
      ]
    }
  }
}

--context ide-assistant trims Serena's toolset to what makes sense inside Claude Code. The old advice to uv tool install it globally and disable the web dashboard still works (web_dashboard: false in ~/.serena/serena_config.yml), but per-project uvx keeps machines reproducible from the repo alone.

docs.title: Google Docs / Sheets — user-level
docs.text:
Local stdio servers (run via uv/uvx) for reading and editing Google Docs/Sheets from sessions. Added with claude mcp add; check status any time:

claude mcp list

docs.title: What I dropped since February
docs.text:
• Sequential Thinking — built-in extended thinking covers it; the extra server was noise.
  • Sentry — never used it; it came from a tutorial, not a need.
  • GitHub MCP — the gh CLI does everything (PRs, issues, API) with less overhead, and Claude Code drives gh natively.

docs.title: 6. Skills
docs.text:
Skills are reusable instruction sets invoked as /name or auto-triggered. Personal skills live in ~/.claude/skills/; I keep the sources in the repos they belong to and symlink them in, so the skill is versioned with the project it serves:

ln -s ~/my-project/skills/my-skill ~/.claude/skills/my-skill

My daily-driver example: a two-phase daily-report system —

  • daily-report-capture — at the end of any work session, writes a digest of that session's work into an inbox directory (fast, no report composition)
  • daily-report — composes the day's digests into a bilingual report pair, lints, commits

The compose step runs unattended at 21:30 via launchd:

# ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.<user>.daily-report-compose.plist
launchctl list | grep daily-report

This pattern — capture cheaply during sessions, compose on a schedule — generalizes to any "end of day roll-up" workflow.

docs.title: 7. Memory: CLAUDE.md Hierarchy
docs.text:
Claude Code reads instruction files at session start, most-specific last:

File Scope What goes in it ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md All projects Cross-project rules: delegation policy, secret-handling rules, server-protection rules. Can @include other files (mine pulls in RTK.md and CODEX.md) <repo>/CLAUDE.md One project, committed Build/test commands, conventions, hard operational rules for that repo Auto-memory Per project, private Claude's own persistent notes across sessions 
# Generate a starter project CLAUDE.md from inside Claude Code:
❯ /init

Keep them concise: delete anything Claude can infer from the code itself. The highest-value content is rules that prevent damage (what never to run, what never to read) and decisions that aren't visible in the code.

docs.title: 8. Permissions & Settings
docs.text:
~/.claude/settings.json controls permissions, hooks, model choice, and the statusline. The shape of mine:

{
  "model": "opus",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(git *)", "Bash(uv run *)", "..."],
    "deny": ["Bash(sudo *)", "Read(.env*)", "..."]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": ["... rtk rewrite + guard hooks ..."]
  },
  "statusLine": { "command": "node $HOME/.claude/hud/omc-hud.mjs" }
}
  • Deny-list reads of secret files (.env*, key files) — the deny rule is cheap insurance against a careless session.
  • Project-level .claude/settings.json (committed) sets team defaults; user-level wins.
  • The statusline HUD comes from oh-my-claudecode and shows model, context usage, and active agents.

docs.title: 9. Verification
docs.text:
# CLI + engines
claude --version && codex --version && rtk gain

# MCP servers all green
claude mcp list

# Plugins enabled
claude
❯ /plugin

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Issue Solution Serena timeout Use --context ide-assistant; if using a global config, ensure web_dashboard: false in ~/.serena/serena_config.yml rtk gain fails Wrong rtk binary installed (name collision) — check which rtk Codex asks for approval constantly Add the repo to the trusted list in ~/.codex/config.toml, or pass --sandbox read-only claude not found The native installer puts it in ~/.local/bin — ensure that's on PATH Homebrew not on PATH source ~/.zprofile or restart the terminal Plugin hooks not firing Re-run the plugin's setup (e.g. "setup omc") after Claude Code updates

Last updated: August 2026 — rewritten from the stock-install guide to document the full working harness (plugins, Codex offload, rtk, per-project Serena, skills, launchd automation).

docs.title: MacBook Developer Setup Guide (2026, M4 Pro)
docs.text: This guide rebuilds my MacBook Pro (M4 Pro, macOS 26) development environment from scratch. Originally written for engineers coming from a Windows/WSL background; as of August 2026 it reflects the machine I actually work on daily — an ML/data-infrastructure setup centered on terminals, Python tooling, and an AI coding harness.

docs.title: 1. Security (Do This First)
docs.text:
Your MacBook shipped with a weak password. Fix this before anything else.

  1. Apple Menu → System Settings → Touch ID & Password → change your password
  2. System Settings → Privacy & Security → FileVault → Turn On (full-disk encryption)

docs.title: Trackpad
docs.text: System Settings → Trackpad: - Enable Tap to click - Enable Three finger drag (Accessibility → Pointer Control → Trackpad Options)

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text: System Settings → Keyboard: - Set Key repeat rate to Fast - Set Delay until repeat to Short

docs.title: Finder: Show Hidden Files
docs.text: defaults write com.apple.finder AppleShowAllFiles YES && killall Finder

docs.title: 3. Xcode Command Line Tools
docs.text:
This installs Git and the compilers that every other developer tool depends on. Run this first.

xcode-select --install

A popup will appear — click Install and wait (~5 minutes).

# Verify
git --version

docs.title: 4. Homebrew
docs.text:
Homebrew is the macOS package manager for both GUI apps (casks) and CLI tools (formulae).

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

After installation, the installer prints two commands to add Homebrew to your PATH. Run both of them, then:

source ~/.zprofile

# Verify
brew --version

docs.title: 5. Apps via Homebrew Cask
docs.text:
This is the full set I run today, grouped by role. Install what you need in one command:

# Browsers
brew install --cask arc google-chrome firefox

# Terminals — iTerm2 is my daily driver; Ghostty and Warp as alternates
brew install --cask iterm2 ghostty warp

# Editors & IDEs

docs.title: 10. Python Environments
docs.text: Never use the system Python (/usr/bin/python3). Manage environments per project.

docs.title: uv — Python projects (the default)
docs.text:
# Create a virtual environment
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# Install packages
uv pip install <package>

# Or, for a locked project workflow:
uv sync            # install from pyproject.toml + uv.lock

cd my-project

docs.title: uv tool — Global Python CLI Tools

# Example: MkDocs for static site generation (this site)
uv tool install "mkdocs>=1.6,<2.0" --with mkdocs-material

# Verify
mkdocs --version

# Common MkDocs commands (run from your docs project root)
mkdocs serve        # local preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build        # build static site to /site
mkdocs gh-deploy    # deploy directly to GitHub Pages

Why pin <2.0? MkDocs 2.0 broke compatibility with mkdocs-material when it landed in early 2026. I still run MkDocs 1.6.x — re-check Material's compatibility notes before unpinning.

docs.title: WSL Dev Setup Guide (Windows + Ubuntu)
docs.text:
This guide sets up WSL2 (Ubuntu) on my personal Windows desktop as a Linux dev environment with Claude Code and the AI harness. It doubles as the generic Linux setup guide — everything from Section 2 onward applies to a native Ubuntu machine too; skip the WSL-specific parts (Sections 1 and 9).

The AI-harness layer (plugins, Codex offload, rtk, Serena, skills) is documented once in Harness_setup.md — the concepts and commands are platform-independent. This guide covers the Linux-side installs and the WSL-specific pitfalls.

docs.title: 1. Install WSL2 (Windows Side)
docs.text:
Run these commands in PowerShell (Admin) — right-click Start → Terminal (Admin). Everything after this step runs inside WSL.

# Install WSL2 + Ubuntu (if not already present)
wsl --install -d Ubuntu

# Keep WSL and the kernel up to date
wsl --update

Verify WSL2 is active:

wsl --list --verbose
# VERSION column must be 2 for Ubuntu

If it shows version 1, convert: wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2.

Launch Ubuntu once to create your Linux user, then close PowerShell. All remaining steps run inside the WSL terminal.

Performance rule: Always keep projects under ~/ inside WSL. The /mnt/c/ mount is Windows NTFS bridged through WSL — it is 10-100x slower for git, node_modules, and file-watching. Never clone repos to /mnt/c/Users/....

docs.title: 2. System Update & Build Tools
docs.text:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y && sudo apt autoremove -y

# Install compilers and core tools needed by nvm, uv, and other installers
sudo apt install -y build-essential curl git wget unzip ca-certificates gnupg

docs.title: 3. Shell: zsh + Oh My Zsh
docs.text:
Ubuntu defaults to bash. zsh gives you Git branch display, tab completion, and useful aliases. This step must come before anything that writes to ~/.zshrc.

# Install zsh
sudo apt install -y zsh

# Set zsh as your default shell (takes effect on next login)
chsh -s $(which zsh)

# Install Oh My Zsh
sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/tools/install.sh)"

Close and reopen your terminal. You should now be in zsh.

# Verify
echo $SHELL
# Expected: /usr/bin/zsh

docs.title: 4. Git + GitHub
docs.text:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your@email.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Generate an SSH key (use your GitHub email), then add the .pub to GitHub → Settings → SSH Keys
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your@email.com"
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Test
ssh -T git@github.com

docs.title: GitHub CLI
docs.text:
gh handles PRs, issues, and API calls from the terminal — and Claude Code drives it natively, which is why no GitHub MCP server is needed anymore.

sudo mkdir -p -m 755 /etc/apt/keyrings
wget -qO- https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg > /dev/null
sudo chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg] \
  https://cli.github.com/packages stable main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list > /dev/null

sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y gh
gh auth login   # GitHub.com → SSH → Login with a web browser

docs.title: 5. Node.js (via nvm)
docs.text:
Do NOT use sudo apt install nodejs — it installs an outdated version.

# Install nvm (check https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm for the current version tag)
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.1/install.sh | bash
source ~/.zshrc

# Install latest LTS
nvm install --lts
nvm use --lts

# Verify (v24+ LTS as of 2026)
node -v

docs.title: 6. Python: uv
docs.text:
Never use the system Python. uv is the default for every Python project; skip conda unless a specific project demands it.

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

# Verify
uv --version

# Per-project workflow
uv venv && source .venv/bin/activate   # classic venv
uv sync                                # or: locked project from pyproject.toml + uv.lock
uv run python script.py                # run without activating

docs.title: 7. Claude Code
docs.text:
# Install Claude Code CLI (native binary, self-updating, lands in ~/.local/bin)
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

# Initialize (follow the login prompts)
claude

Log in with a Claude account (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise) unless you specifically want API-metered billing.

docs.title: The harness layer
docs.text:
Everything beyond the bare install — plugins (oh-my-claudecode, codex), the Codex CLI as a token-offload second engine, rtk, skills, the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, and settings.json permissions — is documented in Harness_setup.md and works identically on Linux/WSL. Linux-specific notes:

# Codex CLI on Linux (no brew cask here) — install via npm, log in with ChatGPT account
npm install -g @openai/codex
codex login

docs.title: Serena MCP (per-project)
docs.text:
Register Serena in a committed .mcp.json at the repo root rather than globally — the machine stays reproducible from the repo alone:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "serena": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": [
        "--from", "git+https://github.com/oraios/serena",
        "serena", "start-mcp-server", "--context", "ide-assistant"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Verify from any session:

claude mcp list

Dropped since the February version of this guide: Sequential Thinking MCP (built-in extended thinking covers it), Sentry MCP (never used), GitHub MCP (gh does it better).

docs.title: 8. Project Memory (CLAUDE.md)
docs.text:
CLAUDE.md is read automatically at session start — project conventions, build/test commands, and gotchas live there so Claude never needs to be told twice.

# Inside your project directory, inside Claude Code:
❯ /init

Keep it concise; delete anything Claude can infer from the code. Details and the global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md hierarchy: see Harness_setup.md.

docs.title: Clipboard — pbcopy / pbpaste shims
docs.text:
Many guides and workflows reference pbcopy (macOS). On WSL, use Windows clipboard interop:

# Add to ~/.zshrc
alias pbcopy='clip.exe'
alias pbpaste='powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command Get-Clipboard | tr -d "\r"'

clip.exe reads stdin and puts it on the Windows clipboard — echo "foo" | pbcopy works exactly like on macOS.

docs.title: Opening URLs and folders in Windows
docs.text:
# Install wslu (Windows Subsystem for Linux Utilities) if not already present
sudo apt install -y wslu

wslview https://example.com      # opens default Windows browser
explorer.exe .                   # opens current WSL dir in Windows Explorer

docs.title: Editors / IDEs
docs.text:
• VS Code: Install on Windows, then add the WSL extension. Run code . inside WSL — the VS Code server runs in WSL, the UI runs on Windows. This is the recommended setup.
  • JetBrains (PyCharm/IntelliJ): Use "Remote Development → WSL" from the Welcome screen. Don't open WSL projects via \\wsl$\... in the Windows IDE — that breaks file watchers.

docs.title: SSH keys
docs.text:
Keep SSH keys inside WSL, not on the Windows filesystem:

# If you have existing keys on Windows, copy them in:
cp /mnt/c/Users/YOUR_USERNAME/.ssh/id_ed25519{,.pub} ~/.ssh/
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Permissions on /mnt/c are faked by WSL and will break SSH's strict-mode check — always store keys under ~/.ssh/ inside WSL.

docs.title: 10. Optional Tools
docs.text: sudo apt install -y ffmpeg jq ripgrep tmux

docs.title: 11. Verification
docs.text:
node -v && uv --version && gh --version && claude --version && codex --version
claude
❯ /mcp        # MCP servers green
❯ /plugin     # plugins enabled

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Issue Solution WSL version is 1 From PowerShell: wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2 Slow git/npm operations Move your project to ~/ inside WSL — /mnt/c is 10-100x slower Serena timeout Use --context ide-assistant in the .mcp.json args claude not found The installer puts it in ~/.local/bin — ensure that's on PATH Node not found Run nvm use --lts or restart your shell zsh not default Run chsh -s $(which zsh) then close and reopen WSL ~/.zshrc not found Make sure Oh My Zsh is installed before running the Node/uv installers WSL paths Use /home/username/... not /Users/username/... (that's macOS) Clipboard not working Ensure alias pbcopy='clip.exe' is in ~/.zshrc and restart your shell VS Code can't see WSL Install the WSL extension in VS Code on the Windows side

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] WSL2 + Ubuntu installed, projects under ~/ (never /mnt/c)
  • [ ] build-essential and git installed
  • [ ] zsh + Oh My Zsh installed and default
  • [ ] Git configured, SSH key added to GitHub, gh authenticated
  • [ ] node via nvm (v24+ LTS), uv installed
  • [ ] Claude Code installed and logged in
  • [ ] Harness layer configured per Harness_setup.md (plugins, Codex, Serena)
  • [ ] Clipboard shims and wslu installed

docs.title: Windows Developer Setup Guide (From Zero)
docs.text:
This guide sets up a fresh Windows 11 machine for C++ development using WinGet, ending with a working Claude Code environment ready for ImGui + DirectX game engine and IOCP WinSocket server portfolios.

All commands run in PowerShell. Right-click the Start menu → Terminal (Admin) for steps that require elevation.

For Linux-side development on the same machine (Python/ML, anything POSIX), set up WSL2 alongside this: WSL_dev_setup.md. The AI-harness layer (plugins, Codex offload, Serena, skills) is documented in Harness_setup.md and applies here too.

docs.title: 1. Windows Update
docs.text:
Ensure the OS and drivers are fully up to date before installing anything.

Settings → Windows Update → Check for updates → Restart if prompted

docs.title: 2. WinGet
docs.text:
WinGet ships with Windows 11 by default. Verify it is available and up to date.

# Verify WinGet is installed
winget --version

# Update WinGet itself via the App Installer
winget upgrade Microsoft.AppInstaller

On Windows 10: open the Microsoft Store → search App Installer → Install/Update.

docs.title: 3. Windows Terminal + PowerShell 7
docs.text:
The built-in conhost.exe is outdated. Install the modern terminal and the latest PowerShell.

winget install Microsoft.WindowsTerminal
winget install Microsoft.PowerShell

Close the old terminal. From now on, open Windows Terminal and switch the default profile to PowerShell (the new v7+, not the old Windows PowerShell 5.x).

docs.title: Allow Script Execution
docs.text:
# Required for install scripts and shell profiles
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser

docs.title: 4. Oh My Posh (Shell Prompt)
docs.text:
Oh My Posh is the Windows equivalent of Oh My Zsh — adds Git branch display and a clean prompt.

winget install JanDeDobbeleer.OhMyPosh

# Install a Nerd Font (required for icons)
oh-my-posh font install meslo

Set your Windows Terminal font to MesloLGM Nerd Font in Settings → Profiles → PowerShell → Appearance.

# Add Oh My Posh to your PowerShell profile
if (!(Test-Path $PROFILE)) { New-Item $PROFILE -Force }
Add-Content $PROFILE "`noh-my-posh init pwsh --config `"`$env:POSH_THEMES_PATH\robbyrussell.omp.json`" | Invoke-Expression"

# Apply immediately
. $PROFILE

docs.title: 5. Git
docs.text:
winget install Git.Git

# Restart terminal so git is on PATH, then configure:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "your@email.com"
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

docs.title: SSH Key for GitHub
docs.text:
# Generate key (use your GitHub email)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your@email.com"
# Press Enter three times to accept defaults

# Copy public key to clipboard
Get-Content "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub" | Set-Clipboard

Go to GitHub → Settings → SSH Keys → New SSH Key, paste, and save.

# Test the connection
ssh -T git@github.com
# Expected: Hi username! You've successfully authenticated...

docs.title: 6. Visual Studio 2022 Community (C++ Workload)
docs.text:
This is the core of your C++ dev environment. The NativeDesktop workload includes MSVC, the Windows SDK, and CMake tools — everything needed for DirectX and WinSocket.

# Install Visual Studio 2022 Community with C++ Desktop workload
winget install Microsoft.VisualStudio.2022.Community --override "--add Microsoft.VisualStudio.Workload.NativeDesktop --includeRecommended --passive"

This installs: - MSVC v143 compiler toolchain - Windows 11 SDK (includes DirectX, WinSock2, IOCP headers) - CMake tools for Windows - MSBuild

Installation takes 10-20 minutes depending on your connection speed.

docs.title: 7. CMake
docs.text:
Visual Studio includes CMake tools, but install the standalone binary so cmake is available in the terminal.

winget install Kitware.CMake

# Restart terminal, then verify
cmake --version

docs.title: 8. vcpkg (C++ Package Manager)
docs.text:
vcpkg manages C++ libraries. Clone it to your user folder so it persists across projects.

# Clone vcpkg
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg.git "$env:USERPROFILE\vcpkg"

# Bootstrap (compiles the vcpkg binary)
& "$env:USERPROFILE\vcpkg\bootstrap-vcpkg.bat"

# Add vcpkg to your PATH permanently
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("VCPKG_ROOT", "$env:USERPROFILE\vcpkg", "User")
$currentPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("PATH", "User")
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("PATH", "$currentPath;$env:USERPROFILE\vcpkg", "User")

# Restart terminal, then integrate with Visual Studio (run once)
vcpkg integrate install

docs.title: ImGui + DirectX (Game Engine Portfolio)
docs.text:
# DirectX Tool Kit (DX11 and DX12)
vcpkg install directxtk:x64-windows
vcpkg install directxtk12:x64-windows

# DirectX texture and mesh utilities
vcpkg install directxtex:x64-windows
vcpkg install directxmesh:x64-windows

# ImGui with DirectX 11, DirectX 12, and Win32 bindings
vcpkg install "imgui[dx11-binding,dx12-binding,win32-binding]":x64-windows

docs.title: IOCP WinSocket Server Portfolio
docs.text:
IOCP and WinSocket are part of the Windows SDK — no vcpkg packages needed. Just include the headers and link the libraries in your project.

// Required headers
#include <winsock2.h>
#include <ws2tcpip.h>
#include <mswsock.h>    // AcceptEx, GetAcceptExSockAddrs

// Required linker dependencies
#pragma comment(lib, "ws2_32.lib")
#pragma comment(lib, "mswsock.lib")

# Verify Windows SDK headers are present
Test-Path "C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Include"

docs.title: 10. Node.js (via nvm-windows)
docs.text:
Do NOT use winget install OpenJS.NodeJS directly — use nvm-windows to switch Node versions per project.

winget install CoreyButler.NVMforWindows

# Restart terminal, then install LTS
nvm install lts
nvm use lts

# Verify (v24+ LTS as of 2026)
node -v

docs.title: 11. Python + uv
docs.text:
winget install astral-sh.uv

# uv manages Python interpreters itself — no separate Python install needed
uv python install 3.13

# Restart terminal, then verify
uv --version
uv run python --version

docs.title: 12. GitHub CLI
docs.text:
winget install GitHub.cli

# Authenticate
gh auth login
# Choose: GitHub.com → SSH → Login with a web browser

gh is also why no GitHub MCP server is configured anymore — Claude Code drives gh natively for PRs, issues, and API calls.

docs.title: 13. VS Code
docs.text:
winget install Microsoft.VisualStudioCode

# Restart terminal — 'code' command is now on PATH
code --version

docs.title: 14. Verify All Installations
docs.text: git --version && node -v && uv --version && gh --version && cmake --version && vcpkg version

docs.title: 15. Claude Code
docs.text:
Claude Code runs natively on Windows (PowerShell) — Git for Windows (Section 5) is a prerequisite. For heavy non-C++ work I run it inside WSL instead (see WSL_dev_setup.md); native Windows is the right choice for the Visual Studio / DirectX portfolio work here.

# Native installer
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex

# Fallback: npm-based install
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

# First run — follow the login prompts
claude

Log in with a Claude account (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise) unless you specifically want API-metered billing.

docs.title: Harness layer
docs.text:
Plugins (oh-my-claudecode, codex), the Codex CLI, skills, the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, and settings.json permissions are documented in Harness_setup.md — the /plugin flow is identical. Windows-specific bits:

# Codex CLI (no Homebrew here) — npm install, ChatGPT login
npm install -g @openai/codex
codex login

docs.title: Serena MCP (per-project)
docs.text:
As on the other platforms, register Serena per project in a committed .mcp.json at the repo root (uv from Section 11 provides uvx):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "serena": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": [
        "--from", "git+https://github.com/oraios/serena",
        "serena", "start-mcp-server", "--context", "ide-assistant"
      ]
    }
  }
}

# Verify
claude mcp list

docs.title: iTerm2 Setup Guide (macOS)
docs.text: iTerm2 is the terminal you reach for when you need deep shell integration, persistent sessions, and fine-grained control. This guide covers configuration from scratch after installing via brew install --cask iterm2.

docs.title: 1. Shell Integration
docs.text: Shell Integration is iTerm2's flagship feature. It marks each command in the scrollback buffer, tracks working directories per-session, and enables the toolbelt.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Open iTerm2, then either:

Option A — Menu (recommended): iTerm2 menu → Install Shell Integration

Option B — curl: 

curl -L https://iterm2.com/shell_integration/install_shell_integration.sh | bash
source ~/.zshrc

Shell Integration injects a small snippet into ~/.iterm2_shell_integration.zsh and sources it from your ~/.zshrc. After restarting iTerm2 you'll see small blue triangle markers on the left of each prompt — those are command marks.

docs.title: 2. Suppress the Login Banner

docs.title: Windows File and Asynchronous I/O (Overlapped I/O)
docs.text: File I/O in Windows starts with three kernel-object-based primitives and graduates to non-blocking Overlapped I/O, with two ways to learn that an operation finished: an event object and a completion routine. The third way, I/O Completion Ports (IOCP) — the model behind most high-performance Windows servers and game backends — has its own post, win-08.

docs.title: Basic File I/O: CreateFile / ReadFile / WriteFile
CreateFile
docs.text:
CreateFile is the universal entry point for files, pipes, serial ports, and other I/O objects. Calling it asks the OS to create a File Kernel Object and returns a HANDLE; no actual disk file is necessarily created.

HANDLE CreateFile(
    LPCTSTR lpFileName,           // path
    DWORD   dwDesiredAccess,      // GENERIC_READ | GENERIC_WRITE
    DWORD   dwShareMode,
    LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES lpSecurityAttributes,
    DWORD   dwCreationDisposition, // CREATE_ALWAYS, OPEN_EXISTING, …
    DWORD   dwFlagsAndAttributes,  // FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL | FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED
    HANDLE  hTemplateFile
);

The dwFlagsAndAttributes field is critical later: passing FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED opts the handle into asynchronous mode. Without that flag the handle is synchronous and Overlapped I/O calls will behave as blocking calls.

docs.title: ReadFile and WriteFile
docs.text:
BOOL ReadFile(
    HANDLE       hFile,
    LPVOID       lpBuffer,
    DWORD        nNumberOfBytesToRead,
    LPDWORD      lpNumberOfBytesRead,  // NULL in async mode
    LPOVERLAPPED lpOverlapped          // NULL for synchronous
);

BOOL WriteFile(
    HANDLE       hFile,
    LPCVOID      lpBuffer,
    DWORD        nNumberOfBytesToWrite,
    LPDWORD      lpNumberOfBytesWritten, // NULL in async mode
    LPOVERLAPPED lpOverlapped
);

Return value is zero on failure; call GetLastError() for the code. For async calls, GetLastError() returning ERROR_IO_PENDING is not an error — it means the operation was accepted and will complete asynchronously.

docs.title: File Pointer (SetFilePointer)
docs.text:
On 32-bit-addressed files the low 32 bits are passed directly:

SetFilePointer(hFile, sizeof(TCHAR) * 4, NULL, FILE_BEGIN);

For files larger than 4 GB, pass a LONG* for the high word and check both the return value and GetLastError() to distinguish a genuine error from the valid INVALID_SET_FILE_POINTER sentinel:

DWORD dwPtrLow = SetFilePointer(hFile, lDistanceLow, &lDistanceHigh, FILE_BEGIN);
if (dwPtrLow == INVALID_SET_FILE_POINTER && GetLastError() != NO_ERROR) {
    // real error
}

Other useful metadata functions: GetFileTime, GetFileAttributes, GetFileInformationByHandle. All take a HANDLE; GetFileAttributes can also work on a path string. Close every handle with CloseHandle.

docs.title: Why Synchronous I/O Is Insufficient
docs.text:
I/O hardware operates largely independently of the CPU. A ReadFile that blocks the calling thread until the disk transfer completes wastes CPU time that could serve other requests. In server workloads where ~60% of operations are I/O, the picture looks like this:

ReadFile call         ReadFile returns
    |                      |
    |<-- thread blocked --->|
                           |
                           v  (thread can finally do other work)

The CPU sits idle during the transfer. For a video player this produces a perceptible gap; for a server handling thousands of concurrent connections it becomes a fundamental scalability ceiling. The solution is non-blocking, asynchronous I/O.

docs.title: The Core Idea
docs.text:
When a handle is opened with FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED and a non-NULL LPOVERLAPPED is passed to ReadFile/WriteFile, the call returns immediately (usually with ERROR_IO_PENDING), and the OS finishes the transfer in the background. Multiple I/O operations can be in-flight simultaneously on the same thread — they overlap:

Issue read A  ----[transfer A in progress]---->  complete
  Issue read B   ----[transfer B in progress]-------->  complete
    Issue read C      ----[transfer C in progress]----------->  complete

docs.title: The OVERLAPPED Structure
docs.text:
Every outstanding async operation must own one OVERLAPPED instance. The OS writes status back into it, so the buffer must remain valid for the lifetime of the operation.

typedef struct _OVERLAPPED {
    ULONG_PTR Internal;      // OS-internal status code
    ULONG_PTR InternalHigh;  // OS-internal bytes transferred
    DWORD     Offset;        // file offset low  (union with Pointer)
    DWORD     OffsetHigh;    // file offset high (union with Pointer)
    HANDLE    hEvent;        // optional event handle for notification
} OVERLAPPED;

Offset/OffsetHigh specify where in the file the operation reads or writes. Because the file pointer concept is per-handle (and therefore shared across overlapping calls), overlapped I/O bypasses it entirely by embedding the position in the structure.

docs.title: Opening a Handle for Overlapped I/O
docs.text:
HANDLE hFile = CreateFile(
    "data.bin",
    GENERIC_READ | GENERIC_WRITE,
    0, NULL,
    OPEN_EXISTING,
    FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL | FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED,
    NULL
);

docs.title: Completion Notification Models
docs.text: After issuing an overlapped request the thread must eventually learn when it finished. Windows provides three models.

docs.title: Model 1 — Event Object
docs.text:
Set hEvent in the OVERLAPPED struct to a manual-reset event, then wait on it:

OVERLAPPED ov = {};
ov.hEvent = CreateEvent(NULL, TRUE, FALSE, NULL);
ov.Offset = 0;

ReadFile(hFile, buf, sizeof(buf), NULL, &ov);

// do other CPU work here …

WaitForSingleObject(ov.hEvent, INFINITE);
CloseHandle(ov.hEvent);

WaitForSingleObject (or WaitForMultipleObjects for many events) blocks until the event is signalled. This is straightforward but each outstanding operation consumes an event kernel object, and WaitForMultipleObjects caps out at 64 handles.

docs.title: Model 2 — Completion Routine (APC)
docs.text:
ReadFileEx / WriteFileEx accept a completion routine callback instead of using the event field:

BOOL ReadFileEx(
    HANDLE                          hFile,
    LPVOID                          lpBuffer,
    DWORD                           nNumberOfBytesToRead,
    LPOVERLAPPED                    lpOverlapped,
    LPOVERLAPPED_COMPLETION_ROUTINE lpCompletionRoutine
);

The callback signature:

VOID CALLBACK FileIOCompletionRoutine(
    DWORD        dwErrorCode,
    DWORD        dwNumberOfBytesTransferred,
    LPOVERLAPPED lpOverlapped
);

Because the hEvent field is unused by the OS in this model, it is free to carry an application-defined value (e.g. a pointer to a per-request context).

The callback is not called on an arbitrary thread at an arbitrary time. It is posted to the calling thread's APC queue (Asynchronous Procedure Call queue — every thread has one), and the OS delivers it only when that thread enters an alertable wait state:

// Any of these puts the thread in alertable state:
SleepEx(INFINITE, TRUE);                 // second arg = bAlertable
WaitForSingleObjectEx(hEvent, ms, TRUE);
WaitForMultipleObjectsEx(n, h, FALSE, ms, TRUE);

When the thread is alertable and there are entries in the APC queue, Windows drains the queue — calling each registered completion routine — before resuming normal execution.

Trade-off: The completion routine always runs on the thread that issued the I/O call. For simple single-threaded programs that is convenient. For a server with many threads it couples I/O dispatch tightly to the issuing thread, making load balancing harder.

docs.title: Next: I/O Completion Ports
docs.text: Event objects stop at 64 handles per wait. Completion routines tie every completion to the thread that issued it. A server with thousands of sockets needs a third model: one kernel queue that collects completions from every handle, and a pool of worker threads that drain it. That is the I/O Completion Port, covered in win-08 — IOCP for Socket Servers.

docs.title: Progression at a Glance
docs.text:
Model Blocks caller? Notification Best for Synchronous (ReadFile, no OVERLAPPED) Yes Return value Simple sequential code Overlapped + Event No WaitForSingleObject Few concurrent operations Overlapped + Completion Routine (APC) No (alertable wait) Callback on issuing thread Single-thread async loops IOCP (win-08) No GetQueuedCompletionStatus Many connections, scalable servers

Study notes based on 윤성우, 《윈도우즈 시스템 프로그래밍》 (book + lectures).

docs.title: I/O Completion Ports (IOCP) for Socket Servers
docs.text:
win-04 built up Overlapped I/O: a request is issued, returns at once, and the OS finishes it in the background. It covered two ways to learn that a request finished: an event object and a completion routine. Both break down once a server has thousands of sockets. IOCP is the third way, and it is the one most high-performance Windows servers and game backends are built on.

This post covers IOCP as the core of a socket server. Part 1 is the mechanism. Part 2 is what a real server has to handle on top of it, which the API reference does not say plainly. In the I/O models series, IOCP is the Windows completion model: the kernel tells you an operation has finished, not that a socket is ready.

docs.title: The scalability problem IOCP solves
docs.text:
Overlapped I/O with events or completion routines leaves two bad options:

  • One thread per connection: 10,000 connections means 10,000 threads, each with its own stack, and a scheduler thrashing between them.
  • A fixed pool waiting on events: WaitForMultipleObjects takes at most 64 handles, so the pool has to shard events across threads and still polls.

IOCP replaces both with one kernel object: a completion port. It is a queue that collects completion notifications from any number of handles. A small pool of worker threads blocks on it in GetQueuedCompletionStatus. The kernel decides how many of them run at once.

docs.title: Creating a port and associating sockets
docs.text:
// Step 1: create the port
HANDLE hIOCP = CreateIoCompletionPort(
    INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE,   // no handle yet
    NULL,                   // create a new port
    0,                      // completion key (unused here)
    0                       // concurrency value: 0 = number of processors
);

// Step 2: associate each socket with the port
CreateIoCompletionPort(
    (HANDLE)hSocket,        // created with WSA_FLAG_OVERLAPPED
    hIOCP,
    (ULONG_PTR)pSession,    // completion key: your per-socket context
    0
);

The completion key is an opaque value that the OS hands back with every completion on that handle. Put a pointer to the per-connection state there.

docs.title: Per-handle and per-I/O context
docs.text:
A server keeps two kinds of context:

per-handle (per-session) per-I/O (per-operation) lives as long as the connection one outstanding operation carried by the completion key the OVERLAPPED pointer holds socket, session state, send queue OVERLAPPED, WSABUF, buffer, operation type (recv / send / accept)

The OVERLAPPED is embedded in the per-I/O struct, and the struct is recovered from the pointer GQCS returns:

struct IoContext {
    OVERLAPPED ov;          // the OS sees only this
    enum Op { Recv, Send, Accept } op;
    WSABUF     wsabuf;
    char       buf[4096];
};

IoContext* io = CONTAINING_RECORD(pOv, IoContext, ov);

docs.title: Issuing a request
docs.text:
DWORD flags = 0;
int rc = WSARecv(s->sock, &io->wsabuf, 1, NULL, &flags, &io->ov, NULL);
if (rc == SOCKET_ERROR && WSAGetLastError() != WSA_IO_PENDING) {
    // a real failure; no completion will arrive for this request
}

WSA_IO_PENDING is not an error. It means the OS accepted the request. From here until the completion is dequeued, the OS owns io and its buffer. Freeing or reusing either before then is the classic IOCP use-after-free.

docs.title: The worker loop, with errors handled correctly
docs.text:
for (;;) {
    DWORD        bytes = 0;
    ULONG_PTR    key   = 0;
    LPOVERLAPPED pOv   = NULL;

    BOOL ok = GetQueuedCompletionStatus(hIOCP, &bytes, &key, &pOv, INFINITE);

    if (!ok) {
        if (pOv == NULL) {
            // No packet was dequeued: the port itself failed (or a timeout,
            // if one was given). Nothing to clean up per operation.
            break;
        }
        // A packet WAS dequeued, but that I/O failed: reset connection,
        // cancelled by closesocket (ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED), and so on.
        // The per-I/O context must still be released.
        on_io_failed((Session*)key, CONTAINING_RECORD(pOv, IoContext, ov));
        continue;
    }

    IoContext* io = CONTAINING_RECORD(pOv, IoContext, ov);
    if (io->op == IoContext::Recv && bytes == 0) {
        // Graceful close by the peer. Only a RECV with 0 bytes means this;
        // a 0-byte completion on other operations means something else.
        on_disconnect((Session*)key, io);
        continue;
    }
    dispatch((Session*)key, io, bytes);
}

ok == FALSE covers two different cases, and pOv is what tells them apart. Treating every bytes == 0 as a disconnect is wrong for anything that is not a receive.

docs.title: What the concurrency value actually limits
docs.text:
The last argument of CreateIoCompletionPort limits how many threads associated with the port may be running at once, not how many exist.

  • When a worker blocks for another reason (a lock, a synchronous call, a page fault), it stops counting as running, and the kernel may release another waiting worker. That is why pools are usually larger than the core count (2 × cores is the common rule of thumb): the extra threads cover workers that block.
  • Waiting threads are released in LIFO order, while packets leave the queue in FIFO order: the most recently blocked thread gets the oldest completion. That thread's stack and cache are still warm, and threads at the bottom of the stack stay asleep (Microsoft, I/O Completion Ports).
  • A thread can be associated with at most one completion port.

So the kernel does not simply "never wake more threads than CPUs". It keeps the number of running workers near the concurrency value.

docs.title: Architecture summary
docs.text:
many sockets ── overlapped WSARecv / WSASend / AcceptEx
                         │  completions queued by the OS
                         ▼
               ┌──────────────────────┐
               │   completion port    │  kernel queue, one per server
               └──────────────────────┘
                         │  GQCS: running workers ≈ concurrency value,
                         ▼        released LIFO
         worker 1 ── worker 2 ── … ── worker N    (any worker, any completion)

docs.title: Part 2 — What a server has to handle
Any worker gets any completion: the ordering problem
docs.text:
This is the property that shapes every IOCP server. A completion goes to whichever worker is free, not to a worker tied to its socket.

  • Receives. Keep one outstanding WSARecv per socket and re-post it only after handling the completion. Two receives in flight on one socket can complete on two workers, and the stream is then reassembled out of order.
  • Sends. Several sends in flight on one socket can complete on different workers in any order. Keep one outstanding WSASend per session, queue the rest, and send the queue with a WSABUF array (scatter/gather) when the current send completes.
  • Session state. Even with one recv and one send in flight, the recv completion and the send completion of one session can run at the same time on two workers. Session state therefore needs a lock or a serialization mechanism.

This is why IOCP servers grow per-session locks, per-session or per-room job queues ("strands"), or hand parsed packets to a dedicated logic thread. The I/O pool is fungible by design, so ownership of state has to be rebuilt above it. Linux's io_uring takes the opposite approach. A ring belongs to one thread and completions come back to that thread, so a server can make the I/O thread and the state owner the same thread. That contrast is the subject of the io_uring post in this series.

docs.title: Accepting connections: AcceptEx
docs.text:
A blocking accept loop on a separate thread works, but it serialises accepts and does not use the port. AcceptEx makes accept an overlapped operation:

  • Pre-create sockets and pre-post several AcceptEx calls, so a burst of connections finds accepts already waiting.
  • Fetch the function pointer once with WSAIoctl(SIO_GET_EXTENSION_FUNCTION_POINTER, WSAID_ACCEPTEX). ConnectEx and DisconnectEx come the same way.
  • After completion, call setsockopt(SO_UPDATE_ACCEPT_CONTEXT) on the accepted socket, or functions such as getpeername and shutdown will not behave. Then read the addresses with GetAcceptExSockaddrs.
  • DisconnectEx(TF_REUSE_SOCKET) lets a closed socket be reused for the next AcceptEx, which saves socket creation under churn.

docs.title: Locked pages, and the zero-byte receive
docs.text:
The OS locks the pages of a buffer while an overlapped operation on it is outstanding. It is tempting to read this as "the NIC DMAs straight into your buffer, so there is no copy". That is not how TCP works. Received segments are processed by the kernel's TCP/IP stack and the payload is copied into your buffer. Pinning guarantees the buffer stays resident for that copy; it does not remove the copy.

The pinning has a cost of its own. 10,000 sockets × one outstanding 4 KB receive is 40 MB of locked memory, held while the sockets sit idle. Locked pages come out of a limited system resource. A server that pins too much starts seeing I/O requests fail, and it competes with everything else on the machine.

The standard trick is the zero-byte receive:

  1. Post WSARecv with a zero-length buffer. Nothing is locked while the socket is idle.
  2. When it completes, data is available. Read it with a non-blocking recv into a real buffer, looping until WSAEWOULDBLOCK.
  3. Post the zero-byte receive again.

It costs one extra call per wake-up, in exchange for locked memory that scales with active connections instead of all connections.

docs.title: Fewer kernel transitions: batching and skipping the port
docs.text:
• GetQueuedCompletionStatusEx dequeues up to N completions in one call instead of one per call. Under load this cuts the number of kernel transitions per completion.
  • SetFileCompletionNotificationModes(FILE_SKIP_COMPLETION_PORT_ON_SUCCESS):
  • When an operation completes immediately, no packet is queued to the port and the caller handles the result inline. This saves a queue round trip per fast operation.
  • Every call site must then handle two completion paths, inline and via the port.
  • For sockets, check the Winsock catalog first. With a non-IFS Layered Service Provider installed, a socket with this mode set may never receive completions on its port (Microsoft KB 2568167). Enable the mode only if every entry from WSAEnumProtocols has XP1_IFS_HANDLES set in dwServiceFlags1. Chromium and the Go runtime both do this check, and both treat the mode as an optional optimisation.

docs.title: Lifetime and shutdown
docs.text:
• Closing a socket causes its outstanding operations to complete with an error, typically ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED. Those completions still arrive and still carry your per-I/O contexts.
  • Free the session only after its last outstanding operation has completed. In practice: a reference count per session, incremented per posted operation and decremented per dequeued completion. CancelIoEx speeds up cancellation; it does not remove the need to wait.
  • Stopping the workers: post one sentinel packet per worker with PostQueuedCompletionStatus (for example a key of 0 with a NULL OVERLAPPED). Each worker exits when it dequeues one.
  • PostQueuedCompletionStatus is also how a server pushes its own jobs into the same queue, which turns the port into a general thread-pool queue.

docs.title: Progression at a glance
docs.text:
Model Notification Who handles the completion Limit Overlapped + event WaitFor…Object(s) the waiting thread 64 handles per wait Overlapped + completion routine (APC) callback, during an alertable wait the issuing thread I/O pinned to its issuing thread IOCP GetQueuedCompletionStatus(Ex) any worker of the pool ordering and session state must be rebuilt above it RIO request and completion queues, registered buffers (later post) —

Part 1 extends the IOCP section of win-04, which follows 윤성우, 《윈도우즈 시스템 프로그래밍》. Part 2 is server practice added on top of it.

docs.title: 네트워크 I/O 모델 0편 — 준비됐다고 알려줄까, 끝났다고 알려줄까
docs.text: select, poll, epoll, io_uring, IOCP, RIO. 서버를 만들다 보면 반드시 마주치는 이름들인데, 따로따로 외우면 금방 섞인다. 이 시리즈는 이 API들을 두 갈래의 한 계보로 묶어서 설명한다. 0편에서는 그 두 갈래가 무엇이고 왜 갈라졌는지만 다룬다.

docs.title: 출발점: 연결 1만 개를 어떻게 기다릴까
docs.text: 서버가 하는 일의 대부분은 기다리는 것이다. 클라이언트 1만 명이 접속해 있어도, 어느 순간 실제로 데이터를 보내는 건 그중 일부다. 문제는 "누가 보냈는지 어떻게 아느냐"다.

docs.title: 1단계 — Blocking I/O: 연결마다 스레드 하나
docs.text:
// 연결 하나를 맡은 스레드
for (;;) {
    ssize_t n = recv(fd, buf, sizeof buf, 0);   // 데이터가 올 때까지 여기서 잠든다
    handle(buf, n);
}

가장 단순하다. recv는 데이터가 올 때까지 스레드를 재우고, 오면 깨운다. 연결 하나에 스레드 하나를 붙이면 끝이다.

그런데 연결이 1만 개면 스레드도 1만 개다.

  • 스레드마다 스택이 있다. 기본 수 MB를 예약하니, 1만 개면 가상 메모리만 수십 GB다.
  • 깨어날 스레드를 고르고 바꾸는 컨텍스트 스위칭 비용이 연결 수에 비례해서 늘어난다.
  • 대부분의 스레드는 대부분의 시간 동안 아무것도 안 하고 잠들어 있다. 자원을 기다리는 데 쓰는 셈이다.

docs.title: 2단계 — Non-blocking + 반복 확인: 계속 물어보기
docs.text:
소켓을 non-blocking으로 바꾸면 recv는 데이터가 없을 때 잠들지 않고 바로 EAGAIN을 돌려준다. 그러면 스레드 하나로 1만 개를 돌아가며 물어볼 수 있다.

for (;;)
    for (int fd : all_fds)                       // 1만 번
        if (recv(fd, buf, sizeof buf, 0) > 0)    // 대부분 "없음"
            handle(buf);

스레드 문제는 사라졌지만, 이번에는 데이터가 없는 소켓에도 매번 시스템 콜을 한다. 1만 번 물어서 3번 데이터가 있으면, 9,997번의 커널 왕복은 순수한 낭비다. CPU는 100%인데 일은 거의 안 한다.

docs.title: 그래서: 커널에게 "알려달라"고 하자
docs.text:
결국 필요한 건 이것이다.

내가 일일이 묻지 않아도, 무슨 일이 생기면 커널이 알려줘.

여기서 길이 두 갈래로 갈라진다. "무슨 일"을 무엇으로 정의하느냐의 차이다.

docs.title: 식당 비유
docs.text:
음식을 주문하고 기다리는 상황을 떠올려 보자.

  • Readiness (준비 통지) — 진동벨을 받는다. 벨이 울리면 "음식 나왔으니 가지러 오세요"라는 뜻이다. 내가 카운터까지 가서 직접 받아와야 한다.
  • Completion (완료 통지) — 테이블 번호를 알려준다. 직원이 테이블까지 차려놓고 "다 됐습니다"라고 알려준다. 나는 먹기만 하면 된다.

docs.title: 코드로 보면
docs.text:
Readiness 모델 — "이 소켓, 지금 읽으면 안 막혀"를 알려준다.

// 1. 기다린다: "누가 읽을 준비가 됐나?"
int n = epoll_wait(ep, events, 64, -1);
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    // 2. 알림을 받은 뒤에 내가 직접 읽는다 (여기서 복사가 일어남)
    recv(events[i].data.fd, buf, sizeof buf, 0);
}

Completion 모델 — "이 버퍼에 읽어놔. 끝나면 알려줘"라고 미리 맡긴다.

// 1. 미리 맡긴다: "이 소켓에서 이 버퍼로 읽어줘"
submit_recv(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
// 2. 기다린다: "끝난 거 있나?"
completion c = wait_completion();
// 3. 이미 buf에 데이터가 들어와 있다. 바로 쓴다.
handle(buf, c.bytes);

docs.title: 무엇이 달라지나
docs.text:
Readiness Completion 커널이 알려주는 것 "지금 하면 안 막힌다" "다 했다" 실제 복사는 누가 내가 알림 뒤에 recv를 불러서 커널이 미리 맡긴 버퍼에 작업당 시스템 콜 기다리기 + recv + send 맡기기와 기다리기를 묶어서 한 번에 가능 버퍼 소유권 내 것. recv를 부르는 순간에만 쓰임 완료될 때까지 커널 것. 그 전에 해제하면 사고 대표 API select, poll, epoll (Linux), kqueue (BSD/macOS) IOCP, RIO (Windows), io_uring (Linux)

표의 네 번째 줄이 completion 모델에서 가장 흔한 버그의 원인이다. 버퍼를 커널에 맡겨놓고 완료를 받기 전에 그 버퍼를 지우거나 재사용하면, 커널이 이미 해제된 메모리에 데이터를 써버린다. IOCP를 써본 사람이라면 OVERLAPPED 구조체와 버퍼의 수명 관리에서 한 번쯤 데어봤을 것이다.

docs.title: 시리즈 내내 쓸 두 가지 비용
docs.text:
API를 비교할 때 "빠르다/느리다" 대신 비용 두 개로 나눠서 보면 훨씬 명확해진다.

  1. 유휴 연결 비용 — 연결은 되어 있지만 아무것도 안 보내는 소켓 하나가, 매번 기다릴 때마다 드는 비용
  2. 활성 연결 비용 — 실제로 데이터가 오가는 소켓 하나를 처리하는 데 드는 비용 (주로 시스템 콜 횟수)

이 두 비용을 기준으로 보면 Linux의 계보가 한 줄로 정리된다.

API 유휴 연결 비용 활성 연결 비용 select / poll 있음 — 매번 전체 목록을 커널에 넘기고 전부 확인 시스템 콜 2–3번 epoll 없음 — 준비된 것만 돌려줌 시스템 콜 2–3번 io_uring 없음 줄어듦 — 여러 작업을 한 번의 시스템 콜로 묶음

epoll은 유휴 비용을 없앴고, io_uring은 활성 비용을 줄였다. 서로 다른 비용을 줄인 서로 다른 단계다. 이걸 구분하지 않으면 "io_uring이 poll보다 100배 빠르다" 같은 비교가 나오는데, 그 차이의 대부분은 io_uring이 아니라 20년도 더 전에 epoll이 이미 해결한 것이다.

Windows 쪽도 비슷한 구도다. select는 Linux와 같은 문제를 갖고 있고, IOCP는 처음부터 completion 모델로 설계됐다. RIO는 IOCP의 활성 비용을 더 줄이려고 나왔다. io_uring이 Linux에서 하려는 일과 같은 방향이다.

docs.title: 연표
docs.text:
연도 사건 1983 select (4.2BSD) 1994 IOCP (Windows NT 3.5) 1997 poll 시스템 콜 (Linux 2.1) 1999 Dan Kegel, "The C10K problem" — 연결 1만 개 문제의 정리 2000 kqueue (FreeBSD 4.1) 2002 epoll (Linux 2.5.44) 2012 RIO (Windows 8 / Server 2012) 2019 io_uring (Linux 5.1)

Windows는 1994년부터 completion 모델이 있었고, Linux는 readiness 모델로 오래 버티다가 2019년에야 제대로 된 completion 모델을 얻었다. 이 비대칭이 두 플랫폼의 서버 설계 문화를 꽤 다르게 만들었다. 시리즈 중간에 다시 다룬다.

docs.title: 시리즈 지도
docs.text:
이 시리즈는 블로그의 분류 원칙을 따라 세 섹션에 나뉘어 있다. 플랫폼과 무관한 개념(이 글과 마지막 측정 편)은 Operating Systems에, 각 API의 동작 방식은 Linux Systems와 Windows Systems에 있다.

편 주제 위치 한 줄 요약 0 개요 (이 글) Operating Systems · os-05 readiness와 completion, 유휴 비용과 활성 비용 1 select Linux Systems · linux-01, Windows Systems · win-07 목록 하나로 전부 넘기기. Linux는 비트맵에 1024개, Windows는 소켓 배열에 기본 64개. Windows 편은 WSAAsyncSelect와 WSAEventSelect까지 2 poll Linux Systems · linux-02 개수 제한은 사라졌지만 매번 전부 복사하고 전부 확인 3 epoll Linux Systems · linux-03 관심 목록을 커널에 남겨두고, 준비된 것만 받기 4 IOCP Windows Systems · win-04 → win-08 win-04의 Overlapped에서 출발한 completion 모델. "아무 스레드나 완료를 받는" 스레드 풀과, 그 때문에 생기는 순서 문제 5 RIO Windows Systems · win-09 버퍼를 미리 등록하고, 요청과 완료를 큐로 주고받기 6 io_uring Linux Systems · linux-04 커널과 공유하는 링 두 개. 시스템 콜 없이 요청하고 완료 받기 7 비교 Operating Systems · os-06 직접 만든 서버에서 epoll과 io_uring을 재본 결과

다음 편은 가장 오래된 select다. 왜 40년 넘게 살아남았는지, 그리고 왜 연결이 많아지면 버틸 수 없는지를 본다.
